title: Design a URL Shortener
description: Walk through the complete system design of a URL shortening service like bit.ly — from requirements to full architecture.

segments.text: Welcome to your first full system design problem. We're building a URL shortener — think bit.ly or tinyurl. It sounds simple, but the details reveal real engineering trade-offs.
First, requirements. We need to handle 100 million new URLs per day, with a 10:1 read-to-write ratio. That means one billion redirects daily. URLs should expire after five years by default.

Let's do the math. 100 million URLs per day over five years is about 180 billion records. At 500 bytes each, that's roughly 90 terabytes of storage. Writes are about 1,200 per second, reads 12,000 per second.
segments.thought_prompt: Can a single database handle 12,000 reads per second? What might help?

segments.text: Two core APIs. POST /shorten takes a long URL and returns a short code. GET /:code redirects to the original URL. Simple on the surface, but the devil is in how we generate that short code.

We use base62 encoding — letters a through z, A through Z, and digits 0 through 9. A 7-character code gives us 62 to the seventh power, about 3.5 trillion unique combinations. More than enough for our 180 billion URLs.

For the database schema, we need a table with short_code as the primary key, the original URL, creation timestamp, and expiration date. A NoSQL store like DynamoDB works well here — simple key-value lookups at massive scale.

The read path is hot. User hits GET /:code, we check the cache first. Cache hit? Return a 301 redirect instantly. Cache miss? Query the database, populate the cache, then redirect. With 10:1 read-write ratio, caching is essential.

The write path generates a unique short code, checks for collisions, then stores the mapping. We can use a counter-based approach with a distributed ID generator, or hash the URL and take the first seven base62 characters.
segments.thought_prompt: What happens if two different URLs produce the same short code?

segments.text: Collision handling matters. If we hash and collide, we can append a counter and rehash. Or use a pre-generated key service that hands out unique codes from a pool — no collisions possible, but adds another component to manage.

For the caching layer, Redis or Memcached works perfectly. We cache the top 20% of URLs — following the 80/20 rule, that covers most traffic. With our read volume, caching alone drops database load by 80 percent or more.

Bonus feature: analytics. Every redirect can log a click event to Kafka. A separate consumer processes these events to track click counts, referrers, and geographic data. Keep analytics async so it never slows down redirects.

Here's the full picture. Load balancer up front, application servers behind it, cache layer for reads, database for persistence, and an async analytics pipeline. A URL shortener is simple to use, but thoughtful to design well. That's the hallmark of great engineering.
